title: Why the Kingdom of Darius, Conquered by Alexander, Did Not Rebel Against the Successors of Alexander at His Death
coreMove: Judge conquest and retention by whether authority runs through removable servants or rooted local lords.
sourcePressure: Machiavelli answers why Alexander's successors held Darius's empire by contrasting two structures: a centralized prince ruling through servants, like the Turk, and a prince ruling among hereditary barons, like France. The first is hard to enter but easier to hold after the ruling family falls; the second is easier to enter through malcontents but hard to retain because local lords remain centers of attachment.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version makes this about Alexander's genius. The writer must keep the institutional contrast visible: servants cannot carry the people before conquest and have little independent credit afterward, while barons can open the gate and later lead fresh movements.

counterintuition: most people assume conquest is about military skill, but actually it is structure
centralized systems are always better than decentralized systems
local leaders are always the problem
tryThisNow: set a timer for ninety seconds and draw your org chart
ask whether your team is centralized or decentralized

exampleSpecs.domain: an intelligence service assessing two rival regimes before a coup attempt
exampleSpecs.audience: analysts deciding whether defecting ministers can bring a capital with them
exampleSpecs.stakes: in one regime ministers are rotated servants with no personal following; in the other, hereditary provincial bosses can unlock roads and later rebel
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The analyst moves the minister photos off the map when no local flags follow them, then leaves the provincial bosses pinned to roads, granaries, and radio towers.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Minister photos and provincial flags cover a wall map under a desk lamp.

exampleSpecs.domain: a medieval military council comparing an imperial satrapy with a baronial frontier kingdom
exampleSpecs.audience: a commander choosing whether to seek local invitations or prepare for a direct field defeat
exampleSpecs.stakes: bribed palace officials may open a gate but cannot carry the countryside, while angry barons can help entry and later make holding impossible
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The commander scratches servant under the satrap's removable badge and baron under the lord's hereditary banner, then changes the invasion plan from intrigue to field battle for the satrapy.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A removable satrap's badge lies beside a stitched hereditary banner.

exampleSpecs.domain: a colonial archive team explaining why one occupied territory stayed quiet and another kept rebelling
exampleSpecs.audience: historians reconstructing administration records without turning everything into national character
exampleSpecs.stakes: the explanation changes if rebellions came from rooted local houses rather than the conqueror's lack of talent
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The archivist places appointment slips in one pile and family land grants in another, then traces rebellions only from the land-grant pile.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Family land grants are tied with string beside stamped appointment slips.

exampleSpecs.domain: a cybersecurity incident team taking over two compromised municipal networks
exampleSpecs.audience: responders deciding whether removing the central administrator account is enough
exampleSpecs.stakes: one network routes all permissions through a central directory, while another has autonomous departments with local credentials that can restart the breach
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: After disabling the mayoral admin key, the lead draws a red box around every local department token still trusted by residents and refuses to call the second network secured.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A revoked admin key flashes red beside six local credential tokens.

exampleSpecs.domain: a humanitarian food program entering two famine zones with different chains of authority
exampleSpecs.audience: field logisticians deciding whether village elders can distribute ration cards
exampleSpecs.stakes: appointed depot managers may lack followers once the capital falls, while clan elders can move families toward or away from the program
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The logistician taps the blank ration-card stack, then marks one route capital servants and the other rooted elders before choosing who must be negotiated with after entry.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Blank ration cards sit beside two colored supply routes.

exampleSpecs.domain: a film restoration consortium acquiring distribution rights from two dissolved studios
exampleSpecs.audience: lawyers determining why one catalog clears quickly and the other keeps producing objections
exampleSpecs.stakes: a studio controlled all rights through one dissolving office, while the other had regional families with inherited exhibition claims
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The lawyer stamps clear on the central studio binder, then stops at the regional ledger where each theater family has its own seal and veto history.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A central studio binder sits beside a regional theater ledger with wax seals.

skillTargets: distinguish servant-ruled and baronial structures from scenario evidence
predict whether entry or retention will be harder based on internal authority
analyze why removing the ruling family solves one structure but not the other
evaluate explanations that over-credit the conqueror and under-read the subject state's structure

tryThisNowSpec: Choose one institution you know from public reporting. Mark which actors are removable servants and which have their own followers, assets, or inherited authority. Then write which danger comes before entry and which comes after.
